title: Capstone Project
text:
Welcome

This is a summary report and walkthrough of my capstone project at Western Governors University.





Photo by David Eluwole from Pexels




Research Question

“Among female homicide victims, can weather conditions, agency population, and location predict whether the victim is Black or not Black?”





Why I Asked It
Other studies have linked hot weather to more violent crime, but these relationships haven’t been studied among female homicide victims.



Scope


15,766 records of female homicide victims whose race is known, from 2017 through 2020, across all 50 states and D.C.
Four public sources: homicide records from the Murder Accountability Project, agency populations from DataLumos, daily weather from the Open-Meteo weather API, and state coordinates from Kaggle
Associations only: the project doesn’t claim that weather or agency size causes differences in victim race





How It Was Built
I followed the CRoss-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM) and did the work in R, in Positron, across three Quarto notebooks: the first cleans and merges the raw data, the second explores it, and the third builds and evaluates the model.



What’s Included


Cleaning

merging the homicide, agency, and weather data

Analysis

exploring the outcome and the predictors

Modeling

logistic regression, evaluation, and practical significance

References

the sources cited in the scripts








Getting Started


Cleaning Notebook

Let’s start with the cleaning script!

title: Cleaning Script
text:
Load the raw data
This script cleans and matches the raw homicide, law enforcement agency, and weather datasets, then saves the final dataset as two Parquet file. Each step stays in the order it was done, including checks that led to later fixes. But first, I’ll load in the required packages.
# Load libraries.

#== packages ==
library(here)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(rmarkdown)
library(sessioninfo)

title: Cleaning Script
section: Filter victims and recode victim and offender race
text:
Filter victims and recode victim and offender race
Now, I’ll narrow the homicide DF to female victims with a known race, using the filter() to keep the “Female” records in VicSex and drop the “Unknown” records in VicRace. Then, the mutate() with the case_when() to collapse the three smaller race groups, such as Asian, into one “Other Ethnic” group in victim_race_collapsed, and the if_else() turns that into a two-group victim_racial_construct: Black or Not Black. The result is saved as the recoded DF, and the nrow() and my custom three_col_check() confirm its size and categories.

victim race recode

# Recode victim race/ethnic into binary constructs.

#== victim side: filter gender, drop Unknown race, collapse categories, binary-encode ==
homicide_recoded <- homicide_renamed %>%
  filter(VicSex == "Female") %>%
  filter(VicRace != "Unknown") %>%
  mutate(
    # (Matt, 2020; Hadley, 2024)
    victim_race_collapsed = case_when(
      VicRace %in%
        c(
          "Asian",
          "American Indian or Alaskan Native",
          "Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander"
        ) ~ "Other Ethnic",
      TRUE ~ VicRace # keeps "Black" and "White" as-is
    ),
    # (Hadley, 2024)
    victim_racial_construct = if_else(
      victim_race_collapsed == "Black",
      "Black",
      "Not Black"
    )
  )

#== view recode dataset record count ==
nrow(homicide_recoded)

[1] 197147

#== check recoded and original race constructs ==
# (Buck, 2025)
three_col_check(
  data = homicide_recoded,
  col1 = victim_race_collapsed,
  col2 = victim_racial_construct,
  col3 = VicEthnic
)

The dataframe's three columns returned.


$first_summary
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  victim_race_collapsed      n
  <chr>                  <int>
1 Black                  72849
2 Other Ethnic            6022
3 White                 118276

$second_summary
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  victim_racial_construct      n
  <chr>                    <int>
1 Black                    72849
2 Not Black               124298

$third_summary
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  VicEthnic                    n
  <chr>                    <int>
1 Hispanic origin          14188
2 Not of Hispanic origin   68915
3 Unknown or not reported 114044


The recoded DF has 197,147 records. Since the earlier victim counts showed 199,567 female victims, dropping “Unknown” race removed 2,420 more. In victim_racial_construct, 72,849 records are Black and 124,298 are Not Black, which is the Other Ethnic and White counts in victim_race_collapsed added together.

title: Cleaning Script
section: Match municipal police to local police departments
text:
Match municipal police to local police departments

final municipal join
Finally, the left_join() matches the municipal DF to the deduplicated DF on city_match and state, followed by the same row-count and agency_population NA proportion checks.

# Deduplicated agency and municipal police subset join.

#== join subsets ==
municipal_joined <- homicide_municipal %>%
  left_join(
    geojson_municipal_dedup,
    by = c(
      "city_match" = "agency_city_match",
      "state" = "agency_state"
    )
  )

#== call the total rows function ==
# (Buck, 2025)
total_rows(
  `Duplicated DF Row n()` = homicide_municipal,
  `De-Duplicated DF Row n()` = municipal_joined
)

Total row counts for each object are: 


   Duplicated DF Row n() De-Duplicated DF Row n() 
                  141096                   141096 

#== check NaN rates ==
sum(
  is.na(municipal_joined$agency_population)
) /
  nrow(municipal_joined)

[1] 0.1409962


The municipal DF has 141,096 records, and the joined DF has 141,096, with no many-to-many warning this time. More importantly, the NA proportion is 0.1409962, or about 14.1%, down from about 84% before deduplicating, since rows without a population were dropped before the join, so a record now goes without one only when its city and state have no local police department row that has one.

title: Cleaning Script
section: Build and save the modeling data
text:
Build and save the modeling data
To finish, I’ll save the modeling DF with arrow::write_parquet() as its own Parquet file in the processed data folder, separate from the final DF’s file. Then, I’ll read it back with arrow::read_parquet() and get its number of rows and columns with dim().

modeling dataset

# Save the modeling dataset as a Parquet file.

#== write to data/processed folder ==
# (Olumide, 2025)
arrow::write_parquet(
  homicide_modeling_df,
  here::here(
    "data",
    "processed",
    "homicide_modeling.parquet"
  )
)

#== display row/col counts ==
## (Olumide, 2025)
arrow::read_parquet(
  here::here(
    "data",
    "processed",
    "homicide_modeling.parquet"
  )
) %>%
  dim()

[1] 15766    35


In conclusion, the saved file has 15,766 rows and 35 columns, one more than the 34 columns of the final DF, since it adds jurisdiction_match.

title: Data Exploration Analysis
text:
Load the data
This script explores the analysis data that the cleaning script saved to see how complete the outcome and the six predictors are, how they’re distributed, and how they relate to each other. But first, I’ll load the packages and read in the Parquet file, homicide_modeling.parquet, which gets its name from being the same file the modeling script reads later, and the .weather_raw dataframe to check the units of the four weather measures, since the analysis data doesn’t include them. I’ll also load the helper functions and the plot theme from the utils.R file.
# Load libraries.

#== packages ==
library(here)
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(gt)
library(sf)
library(lwgeom)
library(tigris)
library(osmdata)
library(ggplot2)
library(sessioninfo)

Summarize completeness and scope
Next, I’ll summarize the five numeric predictors, count the missing values in the outcome and all six predictors, and count the records by year and the number of states to see how complete the data is and which years and places it covers.

summary statistics

Compare jurisdiction by outcome
Each record is labeled Within Jurisdiction if the homicide matches an agency with a recorded population, and Surrounding Area if it does not. Next, I’ll calculate the share of Black and Not Black victims in each jurisdiction group.

title: Data Exploration Analysis
text:
Conclusion
The analysis data is complete except for 2,897 missing agency population values. Since 35.7% of its victims are Black, the model must outperform the 64.3% accuracy achieved by always predicting “Not Black.” However, Black and Not Black victims differ most in agency population. The proportion of Black victims also varies by jurisdiction group (36.7% versus 31.2%) and by state (0% to 82.8%). No pair of predictors is correlated strongly enough to prevent the model from separating their effects, so the data is ready for logistic regression in the modeling script.

title: Model Data Build: Rough & Full Model
text:
Training & testing set
Now, I’ll load the packages and the helper utils.R script.
Before the full model is built, the records are split into a training set (11,824 of the records) for building the model and a testing set (the remaining 3,942) for checking how it does on records it hasn’t seen. The split keeps the share of Black victims about the same in both sets.

title: Model Data Build: Rough & Full Model
text:
Training set
The recipe lists the outcome and the six predictors. It fills the missing agency population values with the median from the training set, and turns jurisdiction location into a 0/1 column the model can read.

build recipe

# Specify the preprocessing steps, and set up the outcome and the six predictors.

#== build the recipe ==
# (Dhana, 2026; Datanovia, 2026a)
homicide_recipe <- recipes::recipe(
  victim_racial_construct ~
    temp_2m_avg +
    relative_humidity_2m_avg +
    rain_sum +
    snowfall_sum +
    agency_population +
    jurisdiction_match,
  data = homicide_train
) %>%
  #== learn the median ==
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  recipes::step_impute_median(
    agency_population
  ) %>%
  #== encode factors ==
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  recipes::step_dummy(
    recipes::all_nominal_predictors()
  )

#== display recipe ==
homicide_recipe

── Inputs

── Operations 


• Median imputation for: agency_population


• Dummy variables from: recipes::all_nominal_predictors()




fit the full model
The recipe and the logistic regression are bundled into one workflow and fit on the training set, so the same steps will be applied when the model is checked on the testing set.

# Fit the full logistic regression on the training set.

#== bundle steps ==
# (Datanovia, 2026a; Dhana, 2026)
full_fit <- workflows::workflow() %>%
  #== glue the recipe ==
  workflows::add_recipe(
    homicide_recipe
  ) %>%
  #== glue the model ==
  workflows::add_model(
    # (Dhana, 2026; Prabhakaran, 2026f)
    logistic_reg() %>%
      set_engine(
        "glm"
      )
  ) %>%
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  parsnip::fit(
    data = homicide_train
  )

#== coefficient table + p-values ==
full_fit %>%
  # (Dhana, 2026; Datanovia, 2026a)
  broom::tidy() %>%
  # (Andrzej, 2020)
  mutate_if(
    is.numeric,
    round,
    5
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Full Model: Coefficient + Z-value + P-value**"),
    subtitle = md("*full predictor table*")

title: Model Data Build: Rough & Full Model
text:
Testing set

evaluate metrics
Now it’s time to score the predictions against the benchmarks set before testing, an accuracy above the 64.3% always Not Black baseline and a ROC AUC above 0.5, along with sensitivity, specificity, and the J-index to show how well each outcome level is identified.

# Score the testing-set predictions with different performance metrics.

#== bundle metrics ==
# (Twomey, 2026)
homicide_metrics <- metric_set(
  roc_auc,
  accuracy,
  yardstick::sensitivity,
  yardstick::specificity,
  j_index
)

#== calculate metrics ==
test_results %>%
  homicide_metrics(
    # (Twomey, 2026)
    truth = victim_racial_construct,
    estimate = .pred_class,
    .pred_Black,
    event_level = "second"
  ) %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Predictions Performance Metrics**"),
    subtitle = md("*before testing*")
  )

The model’s accuracy is 0.63978, which is below the 0.64307 baseline, and its ROC AUC is 0.64748, which is above 0.5. Sensitivity is 0.092395, specificity is 0.94359, and the J-index is 0.035985, so the model correctly labels most Not Black victims but identifies few Black victims. Because both benchmarks had to be met, the model does not meet the success criterion.

title: Model Data Build: Rough & Full Model
text:
Practical significance

predictor practicalness
Next, since the numeric predictors don’t have groups, I’ll build two hypothetical records for each one that differ only in that predictor, one at its 1st quartile and one at its 3rd quartile. The other numeric predictors stay at their medians, and jurisdiction location is set to Within Jurisdiction, the group with most of the records. Then I’ll predict the proportion of Black victims for each record and compare each predictor’s change with the 5.5-point difference.

# Predict the proportion of Black victims as each numeric predictor rises from the first to third quartile.

#== records of predictor change ==
quartile_points <- bind_rows(
  # (Posit team, n.d.)
  expand.grid(
    changed = "temp_2m_avg",
    temp_2m_avg = c(
      46.506,
      73.023
    ),
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = 70.233,
    rain_sum = 2.839,
    snowfall_sum = 0,
    agency_population = 393,
    jurisdiction_match = "Within Jurisdiction"
  ),
  # (Posit team, n.d.)
  expand.grid(
    changed = "relative_humidity_2m_avg",
    temp_2m_avg = 60.887,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = c(
      62.548,
      74.968
    ),
    rain_sum = 2.839,
    snowfall_sum = 0,
    agency_population = 393,
    jurisdiction_match = "Within Jurisdiction"
  ),
  # (Posit team, n.d.)
  expand.grid(
    changed = "rain_sum",
    temp_2m_avg = 60.887,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = 70.233,
    rain_sum = c(
      1.213,
      4.6185
    ),
    snowfall_sum = 0,
    agency_population = 393,
    jurisdiction_match = "Within Jurisdiction"
  ),
  # (Posit team, n.d.)
  expand.grid(
    changed = "snowfall_sum",
    temp_2m_avg = 60.887,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = 70.233,
    rain_sum = 2.839,
    snowfall_sum = c(
      0,
      0.55125
    ),
    agency_population = 393,
    jurisdiction_match = "Within Jurisdiction"
  ),
  # (Posit team, n.d.)
  expand.grid(
    changed = "agency_population",
    temp_2m_avg = 60.887,
    relative_humidity_2m_avg = 70.233,
    rain_sum = 2.839,
    snowfall_sum = 0,
    agency_population = c(
      99,
      1760
    ),
    jurisdiction_match = "Within Jurisdiction"
  )
)

#== predicted proportions ==
quartile_predictions <- full_fit %>%
  # (Dhana, 2026)
  augment(
    new_data = quartile_points
  ) %>%
  select(
    changed,
    .pred_Black
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    percent_black = round(
      100 * .pred_Black,
      1
    ),
    # (Datanovia, 2026b)
    group = rep(
      c(
        "Low",
        "High"
      ),
      times = 5
    )
  )

#== display table ==
quartile_predictions %>%
  # (Muldoon, 2021)
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**Predictor Proportion Change Table**"),
    subtitle = md("*within jurisdiction only*")
  )

Moving each numeric predictor from its 1st to its 3rd quartile changes the predicted proportion of Black victims by about 2.2 percentage points for temperature, 8.0 for humidity, 2.9 for rainfall, -0.4 for snowfall, and 1.2 for agency population. Only humidity changes the proportion by more than the 5.5-point difference, so humidity is the only predictor large enough to count as practically significant by this cutoff, while the others are statistically significant but fall below it.

title: Model Data Build: Rough & Full Model
text:
Model visuals
Then, I’ll plot each predictor’s odds ratio with its 95% confidence interval as a forest plot. Because the numeric predictors are measured in different units, such as one person, one degree, or one inch, I’ll scale each numeric predictor’s odds ratio and confidence interval to its quartile range, the change from its 1st to its 3rd quartile (pakalla, 2020; Noah, 2020), so every odds ratio describes the same low-to-high change used in the practical-significance check. Jurisdiction location stays as is, comparing Within Jurisdiction with Surrounding Area.

odds ratio forest plot

# Plot the odds ratio.

#== forest plot ==
# (Masum, 2026b)
odds_ratio_plot <- ggplot(
  odds_ratio_table,
  aes(
    x = estimate,
    y = reorder(term, estimate),
    color = significant
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#FFB060"
  ) +
  # (Masum, 2026c)
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(
      xmin = conf.low,
      xmax = conf.high
    ),
    size = 0.8,
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  # (Masum, 2026d)
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = sprintf("OR = %.2f", estimate)
    ),
    vjust = -1,
    size = 3.8,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  # (Masum, 2026d)
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "TRUE" = "#275561",
      "FALSE" = "grey60"
    ),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  # (Masum, 2026d)
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    x = "Odds ratio (log scale)",
    y = NULL,
    title = "Odds ratios for each predictor",
    subtitle = "1st to 3rd quartile (Surrounding Area to Within Jurisdiction),\n95% CI on log scale; teal = p < 0.05",
    caption = "Fig.7"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  ggplot_theme

#== display figure 7 ==
odds_ratio_plot







#== save figure ==
ggsave(
  # (Olumide, 2025)
  filename = here::here(
    "output",
    "figures",
    "fig_7.png"
  ),
  plot = odds_ratio_plot,
  width = 12,
  height = 7
)

Scaled to each predictor’s quartile range, all six 95% confidence intervals exclude 1, indicating that every predictor is statistically significant at an alpha of .05, consistent with the p-values in the odds-ratios chunk. Relative humidity has the largest odds ratio: 1.409 (1.335 to 1.487) for a 12.419-point increase. Snowfall is the only predictor with an odds ratio below 1: 0.983 (0.976 to 0.989) for a 0.551-inch increase. The jurisdiction location interval (1.115 to 1.369) differs from the interval in the odds-ratios table by less than 0.001. The predictors rank in the same order as the practical-significance changes, with humidity showing the largest increase and snowfall the only decrease.

title: Model Data Build: Rough & Full Model
text:
Predicted Proportions
Finally, I’ll show the practical-significance results in a paired plot. For each predictor, a line connects the predicted proportion of Black victims at its low value (1st quartile, or Surrounding Area for jurisdiction location) to the predicted proportion at its high value (3rd quartile, or Within Jurisdiction). The steeper the line, the greater the change in the expected proportion associated with that predictor.

practical significance plot

# Plot each predictor's predicted proportion of Black victims from low to high.

#== paired plot ==
# (Datanovia, 2026b; stefan, 2022)
practical_plot <- ggpubr::ggpaired(
  practical_long,
  x = "group",
  y = "percent_black",
  # (Hervé, 2017)
  id = "id",
  order = c(
    "Low",
    "High"
  ),
  fill = "group",
  color = "group",
  palette = c(
    "Low" = "#9d5e38",
    "High" = "#5e2e11"
  ),
  # (L Tyrone, 2024)
  line.color = NA,
  # (Datanovia, 2026b; stefan, 2022)
  xlab = "Predictor value",
  ylab = "Predicted Black victims (%)"
) +
  # (stefan, 2022; russhh, 2017)
  geom_line(
    aes(
      group = id,
      color = id,
      linetype = id,
      linewidth = id
    )
  ) +
  # (russhh, 2017)
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Relative humidity" = "#275561",
      "Jurisdiction location" = "#5497a8",
      "Temperature" = "#70868c",
      "Rainfall" = "#cff5ff",
      "Snowfall" = "#0e6e87",
      "Agency population" = "#10302E"
    )
  ) +
  # (Wickham et al., 2026)
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "Relative humidity" = "solid",
      "Jurisdiction location" = "dashed",
      "Temperature" = "dotted",
      "Rainfall" = "dotdash",
      "Snowfall" = "longdash",
      "Agency population" = "twodash"
    )
  ) +
  # (Wickham et al., 2026)
  scale_linewidth_manual(
    values = c(
      "Relative humidity" = 1.6,
      "Jurisdiction location" = 1.3,
      "Temperature" = 0.95,
      "Rainfall" = 0.95,
      "Snowfall" = 0.95,
      "Agency population" = 1.2
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Change in the predicted proportion of Black victims",
    subtitle = "Each line joins one predictor's low and high value",
    caption = "Fig.8",
    fill = "Predictor value",
    colour = "Predictor",
    linetype = "Predictor",
    linewidth = "Predictor"
  ) +
  ggplot_theme

#== display figure 8 ==
practical_plot







#== save figure ==
ggsave(
  # (Olumide, 2025)
  filename = here::here(
    "output",
    "figures",
    "fig_8.png"
  ),
  plot = practical_plot,
  width = 12,
  height = 8
)

According to this plot, relative humidity has the steepest line, rising from 33.2% at its 1st quartile to 41.2% at its 3rd quartile, the only change larger than the 5.5-point difference. Jurisdiction location rises from 33.2% to 38.0%, and the other numeric predictors change by less, while snowfall’s line is the only one that falls, from 38.0% to 37.6%. So the plot shows the same result as the practical-significance check: humidity is the only predictor whose change is large enough to count as practically significant.

title: Model Data Build: Rough & Full Model
text:
Conclusion
All six predictors are statistically significant, but the full model’s testing-set accuracy (0.63978) fell below the 0.64307 always-“Not Black” baseline even though its ROC AUC (0.64748) was above 0.5, so it does not meet the success criterion. Of the six predictors, only relative humidity changes the predicted proportion of Black victims by more than the 5.5-point difference, making it the only one that is also practically significant.
crumbs: Model Data Build: Rough & Full Model

title: Final Thoughts
text:
Photo by Michael Kyule from Pexels




Findings and Implications


Key Findings


Weather conditions, agency population, and jurisdiction location were all linked to a female homicide victim being Black, but not strongly enough to classify individual victims better than always guessing Not Black.
Only relative humidity was also practically significant, raising the predicted proportion of Black victims by about 8 percentage points.
The findings describe associations, not causes, and the data undercount female homicides.





Recommendations


Violence prevention programs could plan outreach to Black women in the months and places where humid conditions are common.
Future studies should add other factors, such as neighborhood conditions, since weather, agency population, and jurisdiction location alone could not classify individual victims.




Even though the model fell short of its benchmark, the findings remained valid because the methods were carried out correctly.
